1:
That Elihu speaks to Job by name is the first thing noticed. Gill observes that the preceding chapter was addressed to the three friends and this to Job himself, and that none of the friends had ever used his name; the opening word carries the reason, since Elihu has taken their part against nobody and has blamed them, and he is full of matter and uneasy until he has vented it, like new wine ready to burst. Keil and Delitzsch note the same thing, that no previous speaker had addressed Job by name, and make the whole discussion turn on a single condition, that Job attend to its connected contents and not to this or that piece of them. Henry draws out what Job is to gather from it: that this speaker does not join the other three, having already disclaimed their method, so that where they were all in the same song he is trying a new way and asks to be heard entire, since no discourse can be judged until it is heard out; and that he means to make a solemn business of it rather than put in a word by the by to show his wit.

The promise of plain and honest speech is then weighed. Gill explains that the uprightness spoken of is not the theme but the manner, these being the real sentiments of the speaker's mind and not the product of a double heart. Clarke makes the claim higher, that since God has given him his Spirit he will speak from that Spirit alone, laying down no false position and drawing no false consequence, and glosses the second phrase as pure knowledge. Henry suspects the friends of exactly the opposite, that they did not believe in their consciences the things they said of Job and said them to support a hypothesis, which he calls a base thing, to condemn with the tongue for a turn those of whom one secretly thinks well; and he turns the claim of plainness into a rule, that men who speak of the things of God should avoid obscurity, since clearness shows both that they understand their subject and that they mean their hearers good. On the next verse Gill and Clarke both hear the account of the creation of man, Gill taking the clause as a proof of the deity of the Spirit, who formed man as well as garnished the heavens, and Clarke finding the very words of the breath of life in it.

The offer to stand in God's place, and the gentleness attached to it, close the paragraph. Gill allows that men do stand in God's stead, and that Elihu does so here as an advocate undertaking to clear God of the charge of severity; he adds the alternative rendering, I am as thou art, a frail creature accountable to God as Job is. Clarke rejects the received translation altogether: the word taken for according to thy wish is not Hebrew but Arabic with a Hebrew suffix, meaning fellow or equal, so that the line should run, Behold, I am thy fellow, I too was formed by God out of the clay. Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch keep the familiar reading, Wesley noting that Job had often wished for just such a pleader. Henry recalls those wishes in Job's own words, that one might plead for a man with God, with the bargain attached that God's dread should not make him afraid. Gill answers that bargain from Elihu's side, since a man who is neither king nor prince, and has not even age enough to command awe, has no terrible majesty to inject dread; Clarke makes the equality itself the point, that between equals no fear can overawe a man out of conducting his own defence; and Ellicott glosses the last clause simply, that he will deal gently and not be harsh.
8:
The charge is grounded on what the speaker himself heard. Gill notes that it rests neither on suspicion nor on report but on words heard with his own ears. Henry presses the same point further: it was not said to him in private, for then repeating it publicly would have been ill bred, but openly, and what is said openly may be openly reproved, those who sin before all being rebuked before all; when anything is said in our hearing that tends to God's dishonour we are concerned to bear witness against it. Keil and Delitzsch supply the complaint in their own rendering, that he is pure and without transgression, spotless and without guilt, while God finds malicious things against him, counts him for an enemy, puts his feet in the stocks and observes all his paths.

Whether Job ever said it is the question the voices divide on. Gill allows that the words are nowhere recorded in that form, but thinks they did fall from Job's lips during the controversy without being written down, since not everything said on either side was preserved. Ellicott denies it outright: Job never used this language, though several of his statements could be perverted into it, and the misunderstanding shows that even Elihu could not enter fully into Job's position, not grasping that a man is righteous in the measure that he trusts God and is then righteous with God's own righteousness, which was the truth Job dimly perceived and was faintly but surely striving after. Henry stands between them, granting that Job had owned himself impure before God and never claimed to be clean in so many words, yet had said that God knew he was not wicked and that he held fast his righteousness, on which the charge could be built; so that Elihu dealt unfairly in making innocence of all transgression out of a plea of innocence of the great transgression, though men who speak unwarily must thank themselves when they are misunderstood. Wesley defends the charge as far as it goes, since Job meant no such transgression as would justify so severe a punishment, and distinguishes it from the accusations of the three friends, who blamed his claim to innocence because they thought him a hypocrite, where Elihu blames it because it came mixed with reflections upon God.

The answer rests on one proposition. Gill is careful to say what is not denied, that Job was a just man before God and before men and lived soberly and righteously; the fault lies in this one thing, that he pressed his own innocence and attached to it undue reflections on God's dealings with him. Henry makes the same distinction the difference between this speaker and the other three, who would not own Job just at all where this one says only that in saying this he is not just; and he turns it into a rule both ways, that to be just is to render all their due, so that a man is not just toward God who will not acknowledge his equity and kindness in every dispensation. Clarke answers Job's demand for reasons by denying that any are owed, God being sovereign and not to be called to the bar of his creatures, and adds that he is too wise to err and too good to be unkind. Wesley widens the one proposition, that God is greater not in power and majesty only but in justice and wisdom and goodness, so that to censure his judgments is to cast off the awe a man owes his sovereign Lord. Ellicott dissents again, that Job had not striven against God at all but had longed to come into judgment with him, and was striving with the darkness about the throne rather than with the justice of God, which he trusted entirely.
14:
The claim that God does speak is set against Job's complaint that he does not. Henry puts the exchange directly: Job had said that God kept him wholly in the dark and therefore dealt with him as an enemy, and the answer is that God speaks while Job fails to perceive him, so that the fault lies on Job's side and the very dispensations he puts a harsh construction on are meant for his good; it is a token of favour that, the quarrel notwithstanding, God should speak to us at all, and a mark of his design that he speaks to us of our own concerns, again and again, giving another warning when the first is neglected. Gill reads the once and twice as two methods, dreams and visions first and chastisement second, or else as simple frequency, line upon line, one way taken up when another has failed. Wesley keeps both senses and lists the channels, conscience, providence and ministers, adding that God will not gratify curiosity about his hidden judgments but will acquaint a man with his duty.

The dream and the vision are then distinguished. Keil and Delitzsch read the words as describing the first mode, God coming forward as a witness in a man's sleep and using dreams or dream-like visions that rise suddenly within the realm of nocturnal thought, a form of revelation especially usual in the heathen world, which lacks a positive revelation; and they note that both the manuscripts and the accents proceed from the correct assumption that a vision of the night and a dream are not the same notion. Clarke takes them as his first two means and defends the first against ridicule, since many have had the most salutary warnings that way, and to decry all dreams because many are vain would be about as wise as to deny the Bible because many foolish books have been written by men who thought themselves inspired; the second he describes as images presented to the imagination in slumber, or to a man awake in bed and wrapt in contemplation, the darkness having shut out the objects that would otherwise divert the mind.

What the speaking is for is the hinge of the passage. Ellicott states it as the main point of Elihu's whole teaching, that the purposes of God are disciplinary, meant to keep a man from the sin he would otherwise be prone to commit, so that Job might have been a righteous man and still be justly chastened lest he prove unrighteous; the opened ear he glosses as God showing a man the sentence he will seal up against him if he does not repent. Henry says the same by an example, that God opens the heart as he opened Lydia's and so opens the ears, which had been shut against the voice of this charmer. Wesley glosses the sealing as an imprinting of the instruction on the mind, and explains the hiding of pride by the effect of such representations of the divine majesty, which take a man off the admiration of his own excellency and show him his weakness. Clarke insists that the dream by itself does no good, since it is the opening of the understanding and the pouring in of light that make men wise to salvation, and lists what the Spirit uses to that end, serious alarms, penitential pangs, the apprehension of death and judgment, and discoveries of justice and of love. On the preservation that follows, Gill takes the pit both ways, the grave where the body turns to rottenness and the bottomless pit of ruin, since the Lord's people are reproved that they may not be condemned with the world, while Clarke keeps to the plainer sense and reckons how many have been snatched from a sudden accident or from the knife of a murderer by taking such a warning.
19:
The second way of speaking is sickness, and the voices agree on that before they differ on anything. Gill reads the connecting word as marking another method, affliction, which has a voice in it that men of wisdom will hear, and is careful to say that the pain meant is of the body and not a wounded spirit, since it is endured on the bed, where a man might have hoped for rest. Ellicott says the same shortly, that this is the second manner in which God speaks, first by dreams and then by afflictions, and offers rheumatism and gout as what the second clause describes. Clarke numbers it as the fourth of his means and brings a witness, that affliction was in God's hand the cause of David's salvation, who said that before he was afflicted he went astray; he notes that the second clause may be rendered either of a disease in which the patient thinks every bone broken or out of joint, or of a strong multitude of bones chastened even in their vigour. Henry sets the whole against Job's own case, that Job complained of his diseases and judged from them that God was angry, and his friends judged so too, where Elihu shows that God often afflicts the body in love with gracious designs upon the soul, which is what makes this part of the speech useful for the due improvement of sickness.

The patient is then described stage by stage. Henry follows the verses as a case: the pain is not a dull heavy ache but strong and acute, and it turns a bed of down into a bed of thorns, where the sick man tosses till the dawning of the day; it is an inward rooted pain, not in one limb but in the multitude of the bones, which shows what frail bodies we have, pained from causes within themselves without any hurt from outside. On the loss of appetite he draws a lesson against daintiness, that we should not be desirous of dainties since they are deceitful meat and we may be made as sick of them as we are now fond of them. Then the man becomes a perfect skeleton, the flesh that was fat and fair consumed so that it cannot be seen and the bones that were buried in it standing out to be counted, a change a few days of sickness can work in a body, though sickness will not make lean the soul that is fed with the bread of life.

The last verse of the four is a matter of translation. Gill denies that the soul strictly so called goes down to the grave, since at death it returns to God who gave it, and takes the word either of the body or of the person of the sick man, given up by physicians and friends and left at the grave's mouth, which is how Job had spoken of himself. Clarke divides the two words of the verse, the first for the immortal spirit drawing near to corruption and the second for the animal life drawing near to those already buried, and reports a rendering of the second as the Destinies, on the view that the Hebrews had such figures as the Greeks and Latins and the northern nations had, though he thinks the plainer sense more natural. Wesley takes the destroyers for the pangs of death, just ready to seize the man. Keil and Delitzsch use the verse to mark where the argument has got to, that the former case needed only a strengthening of the testimony of conscience by a warning given under remarkable circumstances, whereas this second case is the harder, treating not merely of a warning against sin and its wages but of a deliverance from a death already at hand.
23:
Who the messenger is divides the voices at once. Gill refuses the created angel, and though he grants that angels do attend the saints in their dying moments he adds that this proves nothing for invoking them as mediators; the messenger is rather a minister of the word, by office a messenger and an interpreter of the Scriptures, and such a man is scarce and rare. Wesley makes him a prophet or teacher, there to expound the providence and point out the design of God in it, and notes how few are rightly qualified for so great and hard a work. Henry expands the same reading into a rule about sickness, that when God speaks by afflictions we are often so unversed in the language that we need an interpreter, so that the help of a man who knows the voice of the rod is as needful then as a physician's, and such a one is indeed one of a thousand. Ellicott goes furthest, calling the office a remarkable anticipation of the function since discharged by the Advocate with the Father, and saying that one who holds all Scripture inspired cannot but see here an indication of what God meant afterwards to teach about the mediation of the Son.

The ransom is where the chapter rises. Clarke makes it the atonement, and the thing that gives all the preceding means their efficacy, since without it they would be useless and salvation impossible; he cannot think the redemption of a lost world by Christ is obscurely signified here. Henry says the same more fully, that Christ is both the purchaser and the price, the priest and the sacrifice, that the ransom is of God's own finding, a contrivance neither men nor angels could have discovered, and that God glories in the invention, repeating that he has found it. Wesley keeps that exclamation almost word for word and adds what the way found was, the death of the Son, with the plea that though God might justly destroy the man he will spare him. Ellicott fastens on the same point from another side, that it is remarkable the ransom should be God's to find, as the interpreting angel had been God's to provide, so that what saves the man is not his own righteousness but a ransom found for him; and he observes that such words must have fallen on Job's ear gratefully, confirming his old longing for a daysman.

Whether the recovery is of the body or of the soul is the last question. Gill keeps it bodily and comparative, the man who had been reduced to skin and bone becoming plump again, the withered skin soft, the pale face ruddy. Clarke takes every clause of it spiritually, that the man is born a new creature and returns to the days of his youth by becoming a child of God through faith, prayer being the very breath of that new life, and the sight of God's face the knowledge that he is reconciled. Ellicott will not choose, finding the passage a description of the restoration of a penitent and of a recovery from sickness at once. Ellicott prefers the reading that makes the next verse the man's own confession, that he had sinned and perverted what was right and it was not requited to him. Keil and Delitzsch give the whole of it in their rendering, down to the singing to men and the soul delivered from the pit, and Ellicott adds that the better text continues the confession to the end of the passage, that God has redeemed his soul and his life shall see the light. Wesley takes both senses of that last clause, the endangered life restored and the soul delivered from the pit of hell, with light standing for all good in the vision and fruition of God.
29:
The recapitulation is read as a summary of the methods. Gill takes it so expressly, that God is an operating being always at work in providence, sometimes on men's minds in dreams, sometimes by affliction, sometimes by his ministers, and notes that the word rendered oftentimes is in the original twice, so that when once will not serve he repeats it. Clarke makes the numeral three times over, or, since the form is dual, twice three times, which he takes for again and again, and breaks off to bless God for it. Henry lists the instruments in the same way, conscience and providences and ministers and mercies and afflictions, with God making men sick and making them well again, trying another affliction when one has not done the work and a mercy when neither has, and sending a messenger to interpret both. He also marks the difference between the two methods already described, that the dream was to keep the soul back from the pit, which is to prevent sin, while sickness and the word are to bring the soul back, which is to recover those who have fallen into it. Ellicott calls the verse the very key-note of Elihu's doctrine, that the dealings of God are for education and discipline, and that this is what he wishes to impress on Job.

At this point the catena records a dispute between two of its own voices. Henry closes the summary devotionally, asking what man is that God should thus visit him, and draws two consequences: that we should comply with God's designs and work with him for our own good rather than counter-work him, and that those who perish will be left inexcusable, since so much was done to save them and they would not be healed. Wesley quotes that passage, names Henry as its author and calls the words excellent, and then turns on the second consequence with four questions: how much did God do to save them, did he ever do anything to save them, did he ever design to save them, and if not, how can what was never done nor even designed leave them inexcusable? He lets the objection stand unanswered, so that the two readings are left side by side.

The closing appeal is handled briefly by most and at length by one. Gill and Clarke agree on the first charge, Gill reading it as an instruction to weigh what has been said and attend to what is still to come, and Clarke as a demand for the deepest attention. Clarke adds that the invitation to answer is sincere, since it is the speaker's desire that Job should stand clear of all charges. Henry sets that desire against the other friends, who wished to condemn where this one wishes to justify, and makes a rule of it, that those we reprove we should also wish to see clear themselves, and should give them every encouragement to do it; he adds that whoever would both show wisdom and learn it must hearken and keep silence. Ellicott explains what the justifying would amount to, that Job is to be vindicated before his friends by the argument that his afflictions came not for past sin but as a preservative against a possible future defection, on which ground his case may honestly be defended. Keil and Delitzsch render the four closing verses plainly, the bringing back of the soul from the pit, the charge to listen and be silent, the invitation to answer, and the promise of wisdom if there is no answer. Clarke ends with the manuscripts, reporting that one authority reads according to his righteousness for his righteousness, and that many manuscripts, early editions and versions give my soul and my life where the received text has his, which would turn the close of the passage into the man's own words.
